lines: An oven's dashboard shows one flat, steady line through a long network outage.
The sensor was silent the entire time. The line isn't a measurement from those hours at all.
It's the last real reading, repeated, standing in for data that was never collected.
Not every reading is the same kind of number.
A temperature drifts smoothly. A machine state jumps between a small set of codes. A meter only ever counts up.
Averaging, carrying forward, and summing a difference each belong to exactly one of those three, never to the others.
Worth reasoning through before the next reveal answers it.
One bucket on the grid happens to catch a reading of one state code and then another.
Averaged the same way a temperature would be, what does that bucket report back?
answer: A number that was never a real state at all.
A machine state is a label, not a quantity, so there's nothing meaningful halfway between two of its codes.

lines: Put it to the test directly.
Two state codes land in the very same bucket, and the ordinary average of the two comes back as a number between them.
No machine anywhere was ever actually in that in-between state.
A smoothly varying reading gets a mean over its bucket. A state code gets whichever value was most recently true. A running counter gets the gap between where it ended and where it started.
Three different kinds of signal, three different operations, chosen by what the number actually represents.
Apply a mean to all three anyway, and only one of them comes out meaning anything at all.
A genuine swing in temperature happens precisely during the outage, while nothing at all was being recorded.
Repeating the last known reading straight through the gap erases that swing completely.
A smooth path drawn between the point before and the point after erases it too, just by assuming the opposite: that nothing unusual happened at all.
Agree in advance on how long a gap is allowed to be before it gets filled at all.
Inside that limit, carry the last value forward and say plainly that it was filled, not observed.
Beyond that limit, report the point as missing instead of inventing a number for it, and let any later summary count observed and filled points separately.
What a signal is decides how it gets aggregated, not the other way around.
Averaging a machine's state codes produces a state that was never real.
A value that was filled in is a claim about what probably happened, bounded by a stated limit and marked as exactly what it is.
One more case worth reasoning through before moving on.
A dashboard's line has never once shown a single gap, for any sensor, across an entire year of readings.
Does that unbroken line count as evidence that none of those sensors ever actually went offline?
answer: It doesn't. Sensors and networks fail regularly, that's simply the nature of hardware in the field.
A line with no visible break anywhere in a year is evidence that every single gap already got filled before it ever reached the chart.
